name: Frontal lobe
func: The front part of each cerebral hemisphere. It plans and starts movements, controls speech production, and runs "executive" skills like decision-making, focus, self-control and personality.

levels.kid:
Your **frontal lobe** is the part of your brain right behind your forehead. It is like the boss of a team.

When you decide to pick up a toy, the frontal lobe makes the plan and tells your muscles to move. When you want to grab a cookie but you wait because Mom said "after dinner," that waiting is your frontal lobe helping you be patient.

It also helps you talk. The words in your head get turned into mouth movements here.

The frontal lobe keeps growing for a very long time, all the way until people are grown-ups. That is why getting better at planning and staying calm is something you keep learning as you get older.
levels.hs:
The **frontal lobe** is the largest of the four lobes of each cerebral hemisphere, making up about a third of the cortex. It sits at the front of the brain, resting on the bony floor of the anterior cranial fossa above the eye sockets. Its back edge is the **central sulcus**, which separates it from the parietal lobe, and below it the **lateral (Sylvian) fissure** separates it from the temporal lobe.

Its jobs fall into three big groups:

**Movement.** The strip just in front of the central sulcus, the precentral gyrus, is the primary motor cortex. Areas in front of it plan movement sequences.

**Speech production.** On the dominant side (the left in most people), **Broca's area** in the inferior frontal gyrus turns language into the movements of speech.

**Executive function.** The **prefrontal cortex**, the large front-most part, handles planning, working memory (holding a phone number in your head), attention, impulse control and social behavior.

The prefrontal cortex is one of the last brain regions to finish maturing, continuing into the mid-20s, which is one reason judgment and impulse control improve through the teen years.
levels.college:
Anatomically, the lateral surface of the frontal lobe has three horizontal gyri, the **superior, middle and inferior frontal gyri**, in front of the vertical **precentral gyrus**. The inferior frontal gyrus is split by rami of the lateral fissure into the pars orbitalis, pars triangularis and pars opercularis; the last two form **Broca's area** (Brodmann 44 and 45). The medial surface holds the medial frontal gyrus and the anterior part of the paracentral lobule, and the undersurface carries the **orbital gyri** and the **gyrus rectus**, with the olfactory bulb and tract running in the olfactory sulcus beneath.

Functional regions:

- **Primary motor cortex (BA 4):** executes voluntary movement.
- **Premotor cortex and supplementary motor area (BA 6):** plan and sequence movements; the SMA is active even when you imagine a movement.
- **Frontal eye field (BA 8):** drives voluntary saccades to the opposite side.
- **Dorsolateral prefrontal cortex:** working memory, planning, set-shifting.
- **Orbitofrontal and ventromedial prefrontal cortex:** reward valuation, social behavior and emotional regulation.
- **Anterior cingulate (medial):** error detection and motivation.

Blood supply: the **anterior cerebral artery** supplies the medial surface (including the leg area of the motor strip), and the **middle cerebral artery** supplies most of the lateral surface. The frontal lobe connects to the rest of the brain through long association fibers (such as the superior longitudinal fasciculus and the uncinate fasciculus) and to the basal ganglia and thalamus through parallel loops.
levels.phd:
Frontal cortex is organized hierarchically from back to front: primary motor cortex executes, premotor areas select actions, and progressively more anterior prefrontal regions handle more abstract rules and longer time horizons. Rostral regions such as frontopolar cortex (BA 10) are active when people juggle sub-goals or compare an option with an alternative.

The prefrontal cortex is **granular cortex**, meaning it has a well-developed layer IV, while primary motor cortex is **agranular** and dominated by large output neurons in layer V. Prefrontal pyramidal neurons in layer III form dense recurrent connections. In monkeys recorded during delayed-response tasks, these neurons keep firing during the delay after a cue disappears. This **persistent activity** is a cellular basis for working memory and depends on NMDA-receptor-mediated recurrent excitation.

**Dopamine** from the ventral tegmental area tunes prefrontal circuits through D1 receptors along an inverted-U curve: too little or too much dopamine both impair working memory. Noradrenaline acting at alpha-2A receptors strengthens network connectivity, and stress hormones weaken it, which helps explain why acute stress disrupts flexible thinking.

The frontal lobe sits at the top of **cortico-basal ganglia-thalamo-cortical loops**. Separate loops run from motor cortex, the frontal eye fields, dorsolateral PFC, orbitofrontal cortex and anterior cingulate through matching parts of the striatum, pallidum and thalamus (Alexander, DeLong and Strick's parallel-loop model).

Developmentally, prefrontal gray matter thins through adolescence as synapses are pruned, while myelination of frontal white matter continues into early adulthood. Imaging work links this maturation to better impulse control.
levels.expert:
**Exam findings** depend on which part is damaged:

- **Motor strip:** contralateral weakness with upper motor neuron signs (spasticity, brisk reflexes, upgoing plantar or **Babinski sign**).
- **Broca's area:** **non-fluent (expressive) aphasia**, with effortful, telegraphic speech, good comprehension and poor repetition. Patients are often aware and frustrated.
- **Frontal eye field:** an acute lesion makes the eyes deviate toward the side of the lesion, "looking at the lesion."
- **Prefrontal damage** gives three classic syndromes: a **dorsolateral (dysexecutive)** picture with poor planning and perseveration; an **orbitofrontal (disinhibited)** picture with impulsivity and socially inappropriate behavior; and a **medial (abulic)** picture with apathy and very little spontaneous speech or movement. Re-emergence of **primitive reflexes** (grasp, palmomental, glabellar tap) supports a frontal process.
- Bilateral medial frontal lesions can cause **urinary incontinence** without concern, plus a magnetic gait.

The famous case is **Phineas Gage** (1848): an iron rod passed through his left frontal lobe and his personality changed, shaping how scientists understood frontal function.

**Common causes:** MCA or ACA stroke, traumatic contusions (the frontal poles strike the rough anterior cranial fossa), meningiomas of the olfactory groove or falx, gliomas, and **frontotemporal dementia**, whose behavioral variant starts with personality change.

**Imaging:** MRI is preferred. Olfactory groove meningiomas can grow large before symptoms because the frontal lobe tolerates slow compression; loss of smell is an early clue (**Foster Kennedy syndrome**: anosmia, optic atrophy on one side and papilledema on the other).

**Surgery:** the non-dominant frontal pole is relatively "silent," so it is a common route for tumor removal, but surgeons map motor cortex and Broca's area with **awake craniotomy** and direct cortical stimulation to avoid deficits. Frontal approaches are workhorses of neurosurgery.

keyPoints: Largest lobe; front of each hemisphere, in front of the central sulcus
Contains primary motor cortex, premotor areas and Broca's area
Prefrontal cortex = planning, working memory, impulse control
Broca's lesion → non-fluent aphasia with good comprehension
Prefrontal cortex matures last, into the mid-20s

test.q: Which sulcus separates the frontal lobe from the parietal lobe?
test.explain: The central sulcus (of Rolando) separates the precentral gyrus (frontal) from the postcentral gyrus (parietal).

test.q: Damage to which named area in the left inferior frontal gyrus causes slow, effortful speech with good comprehension?
test.explain: Broca's area (pars opercularis and triangularis, BA 44/45) controls speech production.

test.q: A patient becomes impulsive and socially inappropriate after a head injury. Which frontal region is most likely damaged?
test.explain: Orbitofrontal/ventromedial damage gives a disinhibited syndrome.

test.q: An acute right frontal eye field lesion makes the eyes deviate toward which side?
test.explain: The FEF drives gaze to the opposite side, so when it fails the eyes drift toward the lesion.

test.q: Which artery supplies the medial surface of the frontal lobe, including the leg area of the motor cortex?
test.explain: The ACA runs along the medial surface; ACA strokes cause leg-predominant weakness.

test.q: Working-memory 'persistent activity' in prefrontal neurons depends especially on which receptor?
test.explain: Recurrent excitation through NMDA receptors sustains firing during the delay period.
